Surya Transport, 2-1-460, Maheswar Nagar, Yerraguntla, Andhra Pradesh - 516 309, Scch-17 2 Mvc No.5896/2023 Rep. By Sanepalli Venkataprasad Reddy (Exparte) 2. The New India Assurance Co. texts.facts: The petitioner filed this petition U/Sec.166 of the Motor Vehicles Act claiming compensation for the injuries sustained by the petitioner in a road traffic accident that occurred on 15.8.2023. 2. The petition averments in brief are as under: On 15.8.2023 at about 2.00 p.m., the petitioner was proceeding towards Piler town from Chenchemreddygaripalli in the motor cycle bearing No. AP-27-BQ-0417 in the correct side of Rayachoty-Piler road and when he reached near Durgamvaripalli toll plaza, Piler Mandal, Annamayya dist., Andhra Pradesh one stray dog came across the road and dashed against the motor cycle of the petitioner due to which the petitioner fell down on the road. Further while the petitioner was getting up, one cement lorry bearing No. AP-39-U-1847 came from behind in a rash and negligent manner and ran over the left leg and dragged the petitioner to a considerable distance. As a result, the petitioner sustained crush injuries to his left leg. Immediately after the accident, he was shifted to Govt. Hospital, Piler, after first aid the petitioner was shifted to CMC Hospital, Vellore wherein he was admitted as inpatient and has spent Rs.7,00,000/- towards hospitalization charges, treatment medicines, conveyance, nourishing food and other incidental charges etc., Prior to the accident, petitioner was very hale and healthy and he was working as agriculturist and earning Rs.30,000/- p.m. Due to the accidental injuries petitioner is not able to continue the work and is under complete bed rest and he is suffering from permanent disability. The respondent No.1 is the owner and respondent No.2 is the insurer of the vehicle are jointly severally liable to pay the compensation to the petitioner. Hence, prays to award compensation of Rs.60,00,000/- with interest. 3. After service of notices, respondent No.1 remained absent hence, placed exparte. Respondent No.2 appeared through its counsel and filed written statement by admitting the issuance of policy in respect of the lorry bearing No. AP-39-U-1847 and the liability of this respondent, if any, is subject to terms and conditions of the policy. Further contended that, the accident was caused due to negligence on the part of the petitioner himself and there is no negligence on the part of driver of the offending vehicle. Also contended that the driver of the offending vehicle was not having valid and effective driving licence as on the date of accident. The respondent No.2 insurance company denied the involvement of the lorry bearing No. AP-39-U-1847. Further denied the age, avocation, alleged disability and income of the petitioner. The compensation claimed by the petitioner is highly excessive and exorbitant. Hence, the respondent No.2 prays to dismiss the petition against it. In order to prove the claim petition, the petitioner examined himself as P.W.1 and got marked the documents at Ex.P.1 to 12. Doctor is examined as PW.2 and got marked Ex.P13 & 14. In spite of sufficient opportunities, the respondents have not lead any evidence.
texts.arguments: It is common that soon after the accident that too in a grievous and serious situation as depicted in Ex.P11 & 12 photographs the endeavour is to get the treatment to save the life and limb as such the said explanation offered by the informant for delaying the lodging of the FIR is plausible. Perhaps the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Ravi v. Badrinarayan and others reported in AIR 2011 SC 1226, has observed thus: "The purpose of lodging the FIR in motor accident cases is primarily to intimate the police to initiate investigation of criminal offences. 17. The learned counsel for the respondent no.2 vehemently argued that the IMV report of the lorry bearing No.AP-39-U-1847 is not produced by the petitioner and the MLC details also not furnished by the petitioner as such, there is an implication of the vehicle in this case. As discussed above, the Ex. P3 & 4 discloses that RTA with motor cycle and lorry and the IO has opined as per Ex.P5 about the involvement of lorry and negligence of the driver of the lorry, merely because the petitioner not produced the IMV and MLC register extracts the case of the petitioner cannot be doubted. 18. Further the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 insurance company by relying on the contents of Ex.P6 argues that as the petitioner was not wearing safety helmet and as the petitioner was not having driving license the petitioner was negligent and the contributory negligence has to be considered. In this regard if we verify the wound certificate and discharge summary there is no head injury and it is found that if the driver of lorry bearing No. AP-39-U-1847 maintaining safe distance and if the driver of lorry bearing No. AP-39-U-1847 was in controllable speed the said accident was not going to be caused. To avoid the dog the petitioner has fell down on the road but he has not got any severe injuries due to fall from the motor cycle, but the petitioner got injuries as the lorry bearing No. AP-39-U-1847 ran over on the legs of the petitioner. Thereby no grounds are made out to consider the contributory negligence of the petitioner. The view taken by this Court that the police records are prima- facie proof in support of the case of the petitioner, is supported by the decision rendered in Kishan Gopal and another Vs. Lala and others reported in 2013 (4) T.A.C 5 (S.C.), wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court has categorically held thus: In view of the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal should have considered both oral and documentary evidence referred to supra and appreciated the same in the proper perspective and recorded the finding on the contentious issue No. 1 & 2 in the affirmative. But it has recorded the finding in the negative on the above issues by adverting to certain statements of evidence of AW-1 and referring to certain alleged discrepancies in the FIR without appreciating entire evidence of AW-1 and AW-2 on record properly and also not assigned valid reasons in not accepting their testimony. The Tribunal should have taken into consideration the pleadings of the parties and legal evidence on record in its entirety and held that the accident took place on 19.07.1992, due to which Tikaram sustained grievous injuries and succumbed to the same and the case was registered by the Uniara Police Station under Sections 279 and 304-A, IPC read with Sections 133 and 181 of the M.V. Act against the first and Sangu Srinu Alias S Srinivas Rao vs Surya Transport on 1 March, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20339803/ 6 second respondents. It is necessary to reassert that in a claim for compensation filed under Section 166 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the claimant is expected to prove the incident on basis of principle of preponderance of probabilities and the view taken by this Court is fortified by the decision rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Kusum and others V/s Satbir and others which is reported in 2011 SAR (CIVIL) 319. Further the Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Bimla Devi and others v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others reported in (2009) 13 SCC 530 has observed that, it is necessary to be borne in mind that strict proof of an accident caused by a particular bus in a particular manner may not be possible to be done by the claimants. The claimants are merely required to establish their case on the touchstone of preponderance of probability. Further the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in National Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Krishnappa and another reported in 2001 ACJ 1105, where the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka considering the fact that the rider of the offending vehicle was not examined to prove any contributory negligence on the part of scooterist held that the accident had occurred due to rash or negligent driving by the rider of the offending van. In this regard, I rely on the reportable decision, in Civil Appeal No.2476/2019 in the case of M.R.Krishamurthi V/s New India Assurance Company Ltd., decided on 05.03.2019, the Hon'ble supreme court has held as follows, "We may now summarize the principles discussed above: (i) All injuries (or permanent disabilities arising from injuries), do not result in loss of earning capacity. (ii) The percentage of permanent disability with reference to the whole body of a person, cannot be assumed to be the percentage of loss of earning capacity. In Kajal Vs. Jaidish Chand reported in 2020 SCC Online SC 127, it is held that it would be appropriate to adopt the system of multiplier to award the compensation under the head 'Attendant Charges' as the claimant would require the care of an attendant for the rest of his life. f) Towards loss of amenities and enjoyment of life: The petitioner admitted to the hospital for the injuries sustained by him, which might certainly have deprived his of the basic comforts and enjoyment. The learned counsel for the petitioner relied on the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court reported in AIR 2018 SC 1347 between Jagadish V/s. Mohan and others, wherein it is held as follows; Our yardsticks of compensation should not be so abysmal as to lead one to question whether our law values human life. Awards of compensation are not law's doles. In the case of ICICI Lombard Gen. Ins. Co. Ltd., V/s. Ajay Kumar Mohanty and another, reported in 2018 ACJ 2010 8 In arriving at the quantification of compensation, we must be guided by the Sangu Srinu Alias S Srinivas Rao vs Surya Transport on 1 March, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20339803/ 10 well-settled principle that compensation can be granted both on account of permanent disability as well as loss of future earnings, because one head relates to the impairment of the person's capacity and the other to the sphere of pain and suffering on account of loss of enjoyment of life by the person himself. In the judgment of the Hon'ble high court of Karnataka in M.F.A. no.8625 of 2023 (MV-D) between The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd v/s. Sri. Gummanna and others wherein it is held as follows; 22.One of the grounds urged by respondent No.1 19.1 In this regard, he has relied upon the decision of Allahabad High Court in ICICI Lombard General Insurance Company Vs Smt. Seema Devi and 6 Ors In this decision, placing reliance on the decisions in Khusboo Chirania @ Kanta Chirania Vs Kamal Kumar Sovasaria (Khusboo), National Insurance Company Ltd Vs. Mst. Aisha Bano and Ors dated 14.07.2023 (Aisha Bano) and Smt. Kalpana Madhu Gavali and Ors Vs Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation dated 21.09.2023 (Kalpana), it was held that the compensation granted under the head loss of future prospects should not have been subjected to payment of any interest. 19.2 In Aisha Bano, it was held that future prospects is relatable to an income to be received in the future and as such there could not be any loss to the claimants for the payment of future prospects at the time the deceased met with the accident. Interest is awarded to compensate the loss of money value on account of lapse of time, such as the time taken for the legal proceedings and for the denial of right to utilise the money when due.
